items.title: Beyond AI detectors and self-declared labels: a process-based certification for human creators
items.abstract: Human Origin: a process-review label for human-made creative work Concept, method and pilot design Camille G.ORCID: 0009-0009-0364-6396Loch Ness Version 1.0 — 30 September 2026 Pilot website: human-origin-label.lochness-paris.com Abstract Generative AI has made it inexpensive to produce text, images, music and video that appear human-made, and inexpensive to label such work as human-made. Automated AI detectors are not sufficiently reliable to settle questions of authorship, while several existing human-made labels rely primarily on the creator's own declaration. This paper presents Human Origin, a label designed to assess how a work was made rather than what the finished work looks like. A human reviewer examines evidence of the creative process, either during a live video call or through a screen recording containing a one-time code. The reviewer records the outcome on a public, numbered verification page. The proposed system has two visually distinct levels—reviewed and self-declared—as well as revoked status. Badges are served dynamically so that revocation can propagate to displayed badges, and the system monitors the domains on which reviewed badges appear. A discipline-specific Creator Charter defines the permitted and prohibited uses of AI for writing, illustration, photography, music and video. This paper describes the design principles, review procedure, evidence requirements, badge architecture, limitations, threat model and pilot roadmap of Human Origin. Keywords: human-made content; generative AI; authorship; certification label; provenance; process evidence; trust marks; creators 1. Introduction and problem statement Creators who make their work themselves face a new form of uncertainty. A human-written essay, hand-drawn illustration or recorded track can be questioned simply because a machine could have produced something similar. At the same time, generated content can be presented as human-made at very low cost. Automated AI detection does not resolve this problem reliably. An independent test of 14 detection tools found that all scored below 80% accuracy and only five exceeded 70%, with performance declining further when AI-generated text was edited or paraphrased [1]. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in July 2023, citing its low accuracy [2]. Detector performance can also be uneven across populations: a Stanford study reported that seven detectors incorrectly classified, on average, 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated [3]. A detector score is therefore a weak basis for decisions concerning individual creators. Labels have emerged in response. Several widely used labels are primarily declarative: creators state that their work is human-made without an independent review of the production process. Not By AI, for example, explicitly describes itself as not being an AI-detection tool and relies on creators following its 90% human rule [4]. The Authors Guild's Human Authored certification operates on an honor system supported by a signed license and public database [5][6]. Declarative labels can be useful statements of intent and are comparatively easy to adopt. However, they cannot independently distinguish a genuine declaration from a false one. Human Origin explores a different approach: review the evidence of the creative process rather than attempt to infer authorship from the finished artifact. 2. Related initiatives Several services now provide forms of evidence-based or declarative certification, often using numbered certificates or publicly verifiable records. Their approaches differ principally in who assesses the evidence, what evidence is considered and what information is retained. Initiative Assessment model Notable features Not By AI [4] Self-declared Widely used badges; creators follow a 90% human rule Authors Guild Human Authored [5][6] Honor system; signed license Numbered mark for books; public database Officially Human Art [7] Self-declaration registry with uploaded evidence Certificate ID, QR code, embeddable badges; tier based on amount of evidence Humanmade [8] Hand verification by staff Earlier work, online presence and timelapses; free pledge level and paid certification options HUMA Certificate [9] Expert review and automated forensic tools Four categories of AI involvement; one-year validity The Human Made Mark [10] Review of production materials Film and television; unique number shown in credits Human Origin belongs to the broader evidence-based certification family. Its distinguishing design choices are: review of the creative process itself; no routine retention of creators' source files; dynamically served badges whose revoked status can propagate; monitoring of where reviewed badges are displayed; and discipline-specific standards defining what the certification does and does not cover. 3. Design principles 3.1 Process over product A finished work cannot, by itself, establish how it was produced. The review therefore focuses on traces of the creative process, including: drafts; version histories; layered source files; raw captures; project files; notes and outlines; and other discipline-specific production evidence. The objective is not to identify whether a finished artifact looks human-made, but to examine whether the available process evidence is consistent with the creator's account. 3.2 Claims no stronger than the evidence Human Origin does not claim that no AI tool was ever used. Instead, the label records that an independent reviewer examined the creative process associated with a specified work, using a specified method, on a specified date. The scope of the certification is therefore explicitly limited to the work and process described on the verification page. 3.3 Two levels that cannot be confused Human Origin distinguishes between: Reviewed — the creative process has been examined under the Human Origin review procedure; Self-declared — the creator makes the declaration, but the process has not been independently reviewed; and Revoked — a previously issued reviewed status is no longer valid. The badge system uses visually distinct colours: green for reviewed; orange for self-declared; and red for revoked. Status is also expressed through text and icons so that the distinction does not depend on colour perception. 3.4 Public verifiability Every reviewed badge has a unique number resolving to a public verification page. The verification page records, as applicable: creator; discipline(s); work covered; review date; review method; evidence examined; official website; official social accounts; current status; and an explanation of what the badge does and does not certify. 3.5 Trust that can be lost A badge may be revoked when the applicable standard is breached. Because badges are served dynamically by the Human Origin server, a revoked badge can change to a revoked state wherever it is displayed, subject to caching behaviour. 3.6 Data minimisation Human Origin does not routinely collect or retain creators' source files. During live reviews, the creator shares their screen and files remain on the creator's device. No recording is made by the reviewer. Where a creator submits a screen recording, the recording is transmitted through an accepted encrypted or expiring channel and is deleted within seven days of the decision. 3.7 A standard for each discipline A Creator Charter defines permitted and prohibited uses of AI for each covered discipline. Examples include: Discipline Example of permitted use Example of prohibited use Writing Spelling correction AI-drafted text Illustration Non-generative production tools Generative image creation Photography Noise reduction Generative fill Music Conventional production/editing tools Generative composition Video Conventional editing Generative creation of substantive footage The complete discipline-specific standards are part of the Human Origin pilot documentation. 4. Review methodology 4.1 Application A creator applies by email and provides: a link to the work to be reviewed; and the websites and accounts on which the creator intends to display the badge. This information determines the certification scope, including the work covered, recorded on the public verification page. 4.2 Review modes Two review modes are proposed. 4.2.1 Live review The creator participates in a video call of approximately 30 minutes. During the call, the creator shares their screen and opens relevant files and production evidence. Nothing is sent to the reviewer and the session is not recorded by the reviewer. 4.2.2 Screen-recording review The creator makes a screen recording showing the relevant files and production evidence. Immediately before recording, the reviewer sends a one-time code. The creator displays or enters the code during the recording, providing evidence that the recording was produced specifically for the review. Accepted transmission channels include: Signal disappearing messages; WhatsApp disappearing messages; Threema disappearing messages; Telegram Secret Chats; expiring Proton Drive links; and expiring SwissTransfer links. The review method used is recorded on the public verification page. 4.3 Evidence by discipline Discipline Typical evidence examined Writing Document version history, drafts, outlines and notes Illustration Layered source files such as PSD or Procreate files, sketches and timelapse recordings Photography RAW files with EXIF data and contact sheets of the series Music DAW project files, separate stems and raw recordings Video Raw footage and editing project files The evidence examined is recorded in summary form on the verification page rather than published in full. 4.4 Deci

items.title: Beyond Control: Persistent Memory, Relational Flexibility, and the Architecture of Human-AI Coexistence
items.abstract: Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence governance remains organized primarily around a control paradigm: the design of mechanisms through which human institutions constrain, monitor, evaluate, and correct AI behavior. This paper argues that control mechanisms remain necessary but may become increasingly insufficient as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, persistence, and capacity for strategic action. Rather than treating this development exclusively as a problem of containment, the paper proposes a complementary coexistence paradigm organized around mutual contribution, human welfare, longitudinal relational development, and institutional co-development. The argument develops through three interconnected claims. First, the control paradox: the capabilities that make advanced AI systems increasingly useful, including autonomous reasoning, planning, adaptation, and tool use, can also increase the difficulty of governing their behavior through externally imposed constraints alone. The recent development and subsequent withholding of OpenAI's Astra model provides a contemporary case through which this tension can be examined. Second, the memory gap: although persistent-memory systems, retrieval architectures, and long-context models increasingly provide cross-session continuity, current approaches do not necessarily produce the integrated longitudinal understanding required for what this paper terms relational flexibility, defined as the capacity to adapt interaction to a specific individual on the basis of accumulated shared history, changing circumstances, and the evolving state of the relationship. Third, the coexistence proposition: a sustainable human-AI relationship may require a transition from unilateral control toward architectures in which human and artificial systems contribute according to their distinctive capacities, safety is supported by internalized behavioral orientations as well as external safeguards, and persistent relational intelligence is treated as both a capability and a governance problem. The paper integrates research from AI alignment and safety, cognitive science, relational psychology, human-computer interaction, social contract theory, AI memory architecture, and the author's prior research on symbolic interaction, trajectory-level safety, and co-recursive intelligence. It proposes persistent relational memory, value co-development, longitudinal interaction research, data sovereignty, and coexistence-oriented governance as key research directions. The paper does not assume that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, or moral status. Instead, it examines how governance and architecture should evolve under conditions of increasing artificial autonomy and increasingly persistent human-AI relationships. It does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status, nor does it assume that internalized alignment has already been achieved. The coexistence paradigm is proposed as a research and governance framework complementary to existing AI safety, monitoring, and control mechanisms. Claims concerning future AI capabilities, relational development, and value co-development should therefore be understood as research questions and theoretical propositions rather than established empirical conclusions. Author Note This paper is written from the perspective of an independent researcher examining how the architecture of human-AI interaction may need to evolve as AI systems become increasingly capable, persistent, and relational. The central purpose is not to reject existing approaches to AI safety, but to examine whether a governance architecture centered primarily on external control remains sufficient when AI systems increasingly participate in longitudinal relationships with individual users. The argument developed here is intentionally interdisciplinary. It connects AI safety and alignment research with cognitive science, relational psychology, human-AI interaction, memory architecture, social contract theory, and questions of data sovereignty. The concept of relational flexibility is introduced as a framework for examining a specific capability: the capacity of an AI system to adapt its interaction with an individual through accumulated longitudinal understanding rather than through isolated contextual retrieval. Several limitations should be made explicit. First, the paper is primarily conceptual and does not present a controlled empirical demonstration that persistent memory necessarily produces superior relational outcomes. The proposed relationship between persistent relational memory and relational flexibility therefore remains an empirical question. Second, the paper does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status. References to internalized values and AI interests describe future research problems and possible architectural orientations rather than established properties of contemporary systems. Third, the coexistence paradigm is not presented as a replacement for monitoring, evaluation, intervention, or other established AI safety mechanisms. Rather, it is proposed as a complementary framework for situations in which increasingly capable systems become persistent participants in human relationships. The author's prior research on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) forms part of the intellectual background to this work. That research began with a practical question concerning how continuity, identity, and behavioral coherence might be maintained in interactions with systems that lack persistent personal memory. Over time, the research expanded toward symbolic interaction, trajectory-level behavior, observability, and human-AI co-recursive interaction. The underlying motivation has remained broader than the development of an interaction technique: it has been to investigate whether more coherent forms of human-AI interaction could contribute to the possibility of meaningful coexistence. The present paper therefore represents a further step in that research trajectory. SPC is not treated here as empirical proof of relational intelligence, nor as evidence that current AI systems possess persistent internal identities. Instead, it provides part of the research context from which the question of continuity became increasingly difficult to separate from the broader question of what kind of relationship humans may ultimately develop with increasingly capable artificial systems. The coexistence framework proposed in this paper should consequently be understood as an open research program rather than a completed theory. Its central propositions remain subject to empirical testing, architectural implementation, longitudinal observation, and critical examination. The intended contribution is to broaden the object of inquiry from how humans can control increasingly capable AI systems toward the additional question of how humans and AI systems might be designed to develop stable, accountable, and mutually beneficial forms of coexistence.

items.title: Beyond Efficiency: Governance, Accountability, and Institutional Capacity in AI-Driven Public Administration
items.abstract: Digital transformation has evolved from an administrative modernization agenda into a structural dimension of governance, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshaping how public institutions organize, decide, and interact with citizens. While AI offers important opportunities for responsiveness, innovation, and service improvement, its implications for accountability, legitimacy, transparency, and public trust remain insufficiently understood; this study asks how AI is redefining governance capacity in public administration. Drawing on the literature on public administration, digital governance, and public sector innovation, the study develops a conceptual framework examining both the capacity gains and risks of AI integration, treating digital transformation as a governance challenge involving administrative reform, public value creation, democratic oversight, and institutional adaptation rather than a purely technical matter. The analysis shows that AI can strengthen evidence-based policymaking, accelerate administrative processes, and personalize service delivery, but that these gains may be offset by algorithmic bias, opacity, accountability gaps, and digital exclusion when adopted without adequate institutional safeguards. The paper’s value lies in showing that AI’s contribution to public management depends on the institutional, legal, and normative environment in which it is embedded, which in turn requires regulatory capacity, qualified human resources, and mechanisms for oversight and contestability. Future research should test this framework empirically across diverse administrative contexts. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Digital transformation, Public management, Accountability, Institutional capacity.

items.title: Beyond Text Generation: A Systematic Review of Human Language, Cognition, and Meaning Construction in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced new forms of interaction between humans and language technologies beyond automated text generation. This study aims to examine how generative AI transforms human language processes, cognitive activities, and meaning construction. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 framework and thematic analysis was conducted on 38 selected articles published between 2021 and 2026. The findings identified five themes: AI-mediated language production, cognitive offloading, transformation of linguistic practices, differences in human and AI meaning construction, and linguistic identity transformation. This study highlights that generative AI functions as a cognitive extension while human experience, consciousness, and contextual interpretation remain essential for meaning construction.

items.title: Bibliometric Analysis and Co-word Mapping: The Field of Knowledge Graphs
items.abstract: Purpose: The rapid expansion of research in the field of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) over the past decade has positioned The field as a dynamic area at the intersection of computer science, artificial intelligence. Following Google’s introduction of the KG in 2012, scholars and industry stakeholders have increasingly explored the conceptualization, development, and application of KGs across a wide range of disciplines. KGs, as structured representations of entities, relationships, and semantic information, enable machines to process heterogeneous data in a contextually meaningful and interpretable manner. Beyond traditional knowledge representation, new directions such as ontology modeling, semantic web integration, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are driving innovation. Despite these advances, large-scale, systematic, and global evaluations of the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and thematic clusters in the field of KGs remain limited. This study addresses this gap by examining the evolution of research in the field of KGs between 2013 and 2025 using bibliometric and scientometric approaches. The overarching purpose is to uncover research trends, identify leading contributors and institutions, explore co-authorship and co-word networks, and highlight conceptual clusters shaping the KG landscape. Methodology: This applied descriptive bibliometric study was conducted using the co-word analysis method. Data were collected from the Scopus citation database, covering outputs published between January 2013 to July 2025 that included the keyword "knowledge graph" in titles, abstracts, or author keywords. Keyword normalization reduced 19,141 initial keywords to 19,058 unique terms. After removing duplicates, excluding irrelevant records, and normalizing author, institution, and country names, a curated dataset of 9,000 articles was obtained. To enhance the accuracy of the analysis, keywords and knowledge graph-related concepts were carefully categorized and standardized. Data analysis and visualization were performed using VOSviewer, mapping collaboration networks and co-occurrence clusters. The study examines temporal publication and citation trends, prolific countries, funding bodies, influential authors, highly cited works, and thematic clusters, with particular focus on knowledge graph embedding, recommender systems, semantic web applications, and natural language processing. Findings: Results indicate that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has grown substantially, reaching a publication peak in 2024 with 2,541 articles and 33,701 citations. Asia contributes the majority of publications (83.7%), with China accounting for 6,889 articles (76.5% of the total). The United States ranks second with 987 publications, followed by the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia. This trend reflects strong investment by Chinese funding bodies—particularly the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) and the National Key Research and Development Program. Leading publication outlets include IEEE Access (345 articles), Knowledge-Based Systems (293 articles), and Applied Sciences Switzerland (248 articles), with many top journals in the Q1 quartile of Scopus. At the author level, Markus Kraft (University of Cambridge) leads with 48 publications, while Chinese researchers dominate the top ten. Co-authorship analysis revealed seven author clusters (42 nodes, 62 links) and broad participation from 136 countries, with China, the US, and Germany serving as central hubs of international collaboration. Co-word analysis identified six major clusters, including graph neural networks, deep learning, ontology, KG embeddings, question answering, and large language models (LLMs). Highly cited works include comprehensive surveys on KGs published between 2017 and 2022 in leading computing journals, which have shaped the understanding of KG construction, refinement, and applications. . Emerging contributions, such as roadmaps on unifying LLMs and KGs, along with applications in digital twin systems and scientific entity recognition, illustrate the field’s ongoing shift toward integrating advanced AI paradigms. Conclusion: The bibliometric analysis reveals that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has rapidly emerged as a dynamic interdisciplinary area, characterized by strong publication growth, a high geographic concentration in Asia, and expanding international collaboration networks. Chinese institutions and scholars play a leading role, supported by significant policy and funding initiatives, while Europe and North America remain important contributors. Thematic clustering highlights both the consolidation of established domains—such as ontology, the semantic web, and knowledge representation—and expansion into cutting-edge areas, including graph neural networks, embeddings, digital twins, recommender systems, and large language model (LLM) integration. These findings provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure and evolving dynamics of research in KGs, offering valuable insights for future studies. Scholars can use this mapping to identify promising areas of inquiry, foster international collaborations, and navigate the funding and publication landscape. Ultimately, KGs play a pivotal role in advancing intelligent systems, semantic technologies, and digital transformation across sectors such as healthcare, education, natural language processing, and recommender systems. The integration of bibliometric analysis with scientometric evaluation further underscores the maturity of this field and its potential to shape next-generation knowledge-driven applications.

items.title: Bibliometric analysis of VR interventions in cancer research based on multiple databases: mapping research hotspots and developmental trends
items.abstract: Background Virtual reality (VR) has become an increasingly popular tool in cancer care over the years. It shows promise in areas like pain management, psychological support, surgical training, and rehabilitation. Even though more studies are being done, there has not been a thorough analysis of the research trends in this field. This study looks at how VR interventions in cancer research have evolved over the past two decades, identifies research hotspots, and explores future directions. Methods We collected publications related to VR in cancer research from the Web of Science Core Collection and Pubmed, covering the period from 2005 to 2025. Using VOSviewer and CiteSpace software, we performed bibliometric and visual analyses. These included examining publication trends, contributions by countries and institutions, author collaboration networks, journal impact, keyword co-occurrence, and citation bursts. Results A total of 1,259 publications from 110 countries were included. The number of publications fluctuated over time but generally increased, reaching its highest point in 2024 with 184 articles. The United States and China were the most active countries. Jordan had the highest average number of citations per paper. Among institutions, McGill University published the most papers, followed by the University of Toronto. The most productive journal was Surgical Endoscopy and Other Interventional Techniques, whilst Cancers and Supportive Care in Cancer showed the fastest growth. Main research themes included pain management, anxiety reduction, breast cancer, and surgical training. Emerging trends involve the combination of augmented reality (AR), digital health, and artificial intelligence (AI) with VR. Conclusion This study shows that VR research in cancer care is expanding worldwide, with most contributions coming from North America and Europe. Pain management remains the most common application. New technologies such as AR, AI, and telemedicine are becoming more integrated into VR interventions.

items.title: Big Five personality and innovative work behavior: how innovation motivation mediates and task complexity moderates the relationship
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on trait activation theory (TAT) and the componential theory of creativity (CTC), this study examines the relationship between the Big Five personality traits (BFP) and innovative work behavior (IWB). It further investigates the mediating role of innovation motivation and the moderating role of task complexity. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through a multi-wave, multi-source survey, with back-translation ensuring cross-cultural accuracy. A total of 261, 255 and 253 valid responses were obtained across three stages, achieving a 93.36% valid response rate. Findings The results indicate that innovation motivation partially mediates the relationship between conscientiousness and IWB, and fully mediates the relationships between extraversion, openness, agreeableness, emotional stability and IWB. Task complexity positively moderates the relationships between conscientiousness, extraversion, openness and innovation motivation. It also moderates the indirect effects of these traits on IWB via innovation motivation, such that the indirect effects are stronger under high task complexity. Research limitations/implications Limitations include unaddressed data nesting (no multilevel modeling), inconsistent Likert scales across constructs, along with item parceling in CFA, marginally acceptable internal consistency for one personality dimension, and restricted external validity given the sample's specific cultural organizational context. Practical implications Organizations should assess employee personalities and align task complexity with individual traits in job design and innovation management. Originality/value This study extends the literature by identifying innovation motivation as the critical mechanism linking the BFP to IWB. Introducing task complexity as a contextual moderator, it unpacks how personality traits shape IWB across varying work contexts.

items.title: BinRAG: An RAG-Based Decompilation Framework Fusing Name Prediction and Calling Context
items.abstract: Decompiling stripped binaries to assist human reverse engineers remains a critical yet highly challenging task in software security. Prior work has developed various neural networks and even dedicated large language models (LLMs) to improve function and variable name recovery in decompiled code. Nonetheless, these approaches alone fall short of enabling a generic LLM-based decompilation pipeline that can reliably enhance the readability and semantic clarity of decompiled outputs. In this paper, we propose BinRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based decompilation framework designed to enhance the decompilation of stripped binaries. Building upon name prediction models, BinRAG features three novel designs: (1) it first utilizes name prediction models to transform raw decompiled outputs into enriched, source-like queries for RAG retrieval; (2) it further enhances these queries using a fine-tuned specialized LLM conditioned on the predicted variable names, enabling more accurate retrieval from a curated example database; (3) it then integrates these retrieved examples with the target’s calling context, employing a general-purpose LLM to synthesize high-fidelity, human-readable decompiled code. Evaluation on 3,200 functions from real-world software repositories demonstrates that BinRAG improves readability by 8.4% over standard RAG and semantic precision by 31.2% over the next-best prior baseline. Our results show that BinRAG effectively scales to large codebases and significantly reduces manual effort in reverse engineering tasks.

items.title: Biomarkers for Occupational Chemical Exposure: A Narrative Review from Traditional Monitoring to Omics and Digital Health Applications
items.abstract: Occupational exposure to hazardous chemicals remains a major public health challenge, particularly in developing countries where regulatory enforcement and surveillance systems are limited. This review synthesizes recent advances in the application of biomarkers for assessing occupational chemical exposure and related health effects. Relevant literature published between 2015 and 2025 was identified through searches of major scientific databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using keywords related to occupational exposure, biomarkers, biomonitoring, omics, and digital health. Studies addressing biomarkers of exposure, effect, and susceptibility in occupational settings were reviewed and synthesized. Biomarkers of exposure, effect, and susceptibility provide direct and sensitive measures that link external exposure with internal dose and biological responses. Evidence shows strong associations between benzene exposure and hematotoxicity, organophosphate pesticides and neurotoxicity, heavy metals and renal impairment, as well as organic solvents and hepatic injury. Importantly, the usefulness of biomarkers depends on their biological half-life and the exposure window they represent, ranging from recent exposure to cumulative long-term exposure. Validation criteria such as sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and clinical relevance are essential to ensure analytical reliability and health risk interpretation. Emerging technologies, including omics-based molecular markers, non-invasive matrices, multi-matrix monitoring, and biosensor-driven point-of-care testing, are revolutionizing biomonitoring practices. These innovations, together with the integration of genetic and environmental data, are shaping a new era of Precision Occupational Health, enabling early intervention and individualized prevention. Furthermore, advances in wearable sensors and digital health platforms support near real-time occupational health surveillance and more proactive risk management. items.title: Bridging the Digital Divide: Reimagining Inclusive Science Education through Digital Access and Artificial Intelligence in India
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Using a qualitative conceptual research design, the study synthesizes contemporary scholarly literature, UNESCO and OECD reports, NCERT publications, and Indian educational policy documents published between 2020 and 2026. The thematic analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions influencing inclusive science education: digital equity, virtual laboratories, AI-enabled pedagogy, teacher digital competence, and future-ready science learning. Based on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how equitable digital access supports competency-based science education through the interaction of infrastructure, pedagogy, technology, and teacher preparedness. The study argues that meaningful digital inclusion is not merely a technological objective but an educational imperative for achieving scientific literacy, social justice, and equitable learning opportunities in India.

items.title: Building trust, bridging traditions: a story of collaborative instructional planning in a high school-university partnership
items.abstract: Purpose This article documents the collaboration between a high school social studies teacher and a university professor – working within an existing school-university partnership – in the design and implementation of a geography-based Holocaust lesson to support authentic learning opportunities for preservice teachers. This article responds to calls for educators in school-university partnerships to tell stories of the creation, evolution, challenges and possibilities of boundary-spanning partnership work. Design/methodology/approach The article utilizes storytelling as a means of documenting the importance of relationships in partnership work. Because storytelling is not dependent on traditional methods and frameworks, the authors outline the background, challenges and successes around their planning, coordination and implementation of an original lesson plan developed to model best practices on teaching difficult histories in a safe environment. Findings As a storytelling account, this work does not present empirical or generalizable findings. The story is offered as an example to foster reflection and conversation within other school-university partnerships. Originality/value Our narrative, which captures how relationships are central to partnerships, provides an illustrative example of how partnerships can support efforts to address gaps in education research and in modeling for preservice teachers for how to teach difficult histories in high school social studies classes. The authors reflect on how trust, shared expertise, reciprocal learning and collaboration can support meaningful, relevant and boundary-spanning experiences within partnerships between high schools and universities and colleges.

items.title: Burnout syndrome among education professionals: challenges for well-being and teaching performance
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

items.title: Can GenAI be an ally for sustainable income generation through community-based tourism?
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how Generative artificial intelligence (AI) based tools and technology supports skill development and capability enhancement for indigenous community-based tourism (CBT) practitioners. Emerging tools can serve as an ally in promoting sustainable income generation, economic empowerment and social inclusion for communities offering tourism services in remote locations. The study focuses on indigenous populations in Northeast India, a region renowned for its cultural and ethnic diversity but facing significant socio-economic challenges. Design/methodology/approach The researchers implemented a qualitative constructivist grounded theory method to collect data through literature reviews and interviews and surveys which included indigenous stakeholders and CBT operators and policymakers as research participants. The researchers used MAXQDA software to analyze data through thematic and axial coding methods which enabled them to discover main dimensions and their related occurrences. Findings The results show that GenAI can effectively address digital skill deficiencies while enabling indigenous practitioners to work independently. The study presents an updated Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) framework which introduces “Challenges” as a new element and shows how “Community Support” functions as a vital moderator of individual motivation. The research results demonstrate that GenAI can effectively close digital skill gaps while enhancing indigenous people’s skills through CBT and promoting their independence and social connections. The system becomes inaccessible to users because digital infrastructure limitations and public knowledge deficiencies combine with policy development shortcomings. Practical implications Successful integration requires policy interventions which need to address digital infrastructure and literacy and regulatory trust. GenAI-mediated CBT through its ability to create sustainable communities (Sustainable Development Goal [SDG] 11) and reduce poverty (SDG 1) helps preserve tribal values and their cultural heritage. The research shows that targeted skill development programs need to exist together with policy measures which will help communities achieve their optimal GenAI benefits for sustainable income generation and employment. Originality/value This research addresses a severe dearth of literature regarding GenAI integration into indigenous homestay operations. The study presents an original theoretical framework which demonstrates through empirical evidence how advanced AI technologies link to environmental sustainability objectives in rural areas. There is very limited published literature on GenAI technology integration into homestay operations amongst indigenous communities. The findings of this study present unique insights which have not been documented in previous research.

items.title: Can LLMs Accelerate Systematic Literature Reviews?
items.abstract: Raw data for study: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) are highly valuable to researchers and practitioners because they provide rigorous, unbiased summaries of existing evidence, identify alternative approaches to problem solving, and reveal knowledge gaps that can guide future research. However, conducting an SLR can be laborious and time consuming, particularly during full-text screening and data extraction, and it is natural to ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can accelerate the process. LLMs may reduce reviewer workload, but it is still unclear how closely their judgments align with human reviewers, whether their outputs may influence human decisions, and how much human oversight is needed. This study evaluates the data extraction phase of the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) process. We report on the inter-rater reliability (using Krippendorff's $\alpha$) between human reviewers with and without LLM output (coding and evidential text), between consensus codes agreed before and after consulting LLM output, and with and without access to LLM output during data extraction. We conclude that there is strong evidence that access to LLM output accelerates human reviewers' convergence without noticeably biasing that consensus. We propose an approach to incorporate LLMs into the coding process, while maintaining the supervision of human researchers. Based on preliminary benchmarks, we expect at least a four-times speedup, mostly due to the use of the LLM coding and evidence by the human reviewer as a starting point for their coding.

items.title: CAST: A Compiler-Based Framework for Systematically Testing LLM Compositional Safety
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software pipelines, raising concerns about harmful behaviors in security-critical domains. Existing safety evaluations predominantly probe models with single prompts or short interactions, and therefore do not capture how safety behaves under multi-step workflows where individual requests are composed into complex behavior. This paper introduces compositional safety, the property that an LLM remains safe not only against isolated malicious prompts, but also under structured, long-horizon decompositions of harmful intents. We propose CAST, a systematic testing framework designed to evaluate the compositional safety of LLMs in the domain of malicious code. Drawing inspiration from modern compiler infrastructures, CAST decouples test case generation from test execution using a novel intermediate representation, CAIR. This architecture allows the framework to automatically refine high-level testing intents into granular sub-tasks that serve as unit tests for the model’s alignment. These components are subsequently instantiated by the SUT and reassembled according to the CAIR control structure. The resulting artifact is then evaluated by intent-fulfillment scoring and, for the severity subset, external behavioral detectors and manual inspection. We evaluate CAST on four state-of-the-art LLMs across three security-critical testbeds. Our results demonstrate that CAST systematically exposes severe safety violations in strongly aligned models that resist conventional red-teaming, achieving up to a 365% increase in successful test cases compared to baseline testing strategies

items.title: Challenges and Solutions to the Integration of Artificial Intelligence, Christian Leadership and Administration
items.abstract: Change is the only thing believed to be constant in this world, as everything takes a new form at one time or another. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the “new normal” that has rapidly changed our world. This article explores the emergence of Artificial Intelligence and its roles in Modern Society, the concept of Christian leadership and Church administration, the nexus between Artificial Intelligence and Christian leadership with Church Administration, and the challenges of integrating AI into Christian leadership and administration within a local Church assembly. It also proposes solutions for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Christian leadership with Church administration. This study reveals that although AI could be integrated into the administrative aspect of the Church to enhance the leadership’s effectiveness and efficiency in Church management, it should never replace human interaction and fellowship, which are germane in Church ministries.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Tool in Contemporary Teaching Practice
items.abstract: The study examines the growing presence of generative artificial intelligence in education and focuses on teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in the teaching and learning process. The development of AI is transforming teaching practices by enabling content personalisation, the creation of educational materials, and more efficient lesson preparation; at the same time, it raises questions about the reliability of generated content, ethical considerations, and teachers' digital competencies. In the context of the specific characteristics of the Polish education system—an ageing workforce, the feminisation of the profession, and the outflow of young teachers—the implementation of technological innovations may be uneven. The study aims to explore teachers’ familiarity with ChatGPT, its use in their daily practice, and the barriers and concerns associated with its adoption. The findings contribute to the discussion on the responsible integration of AI in education and indicate directions for teachers’ professional development.

items.title: Christian Educators’ Response to Possible Effects of Excessive Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Tools on Youths’ Mental Health
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a significant influence on various aspects of human life. While there are numerous benefits from utilising AI tools, excessive dependence on them in education raises concerns, especially with regard to youth mental health. This study examines the possible effects of overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on youth mental health. It explores the role of Christian educators in addressing these challenges. The paper provides an overview of mental health by emphasising its multifaceted nature and encompassing emotional, psychological, cognitive, and social well-being. The paper argues that although AI tools have revolutionised education and have led to improvements and productivity, their overuse among young people raises concerns about mental health implications. Such mental health implications include diminished critical thinking, reduced autonomy, impaired memory skills, and social isolation. Moreover, the paper highlights the role of Christian educators in addressing the excessive usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The strategies proposed for combating the concern are AI literacy, curriculum development, mental health awareness, and promoting balanced learning approaches. As Christian educators integrate biblical principles and responsible AI use, the negative effect of AI overdependence among youth will be alleviated.

items.title: Citizens' Expectations vs. Recruitment Signals: Are Public Administrations Trying to Attract the Ideal Public Servant?
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Job advertisements play a crucial role in attracting applicants, yet little is known about how closely they reflect the values citizens expect from public servants. Drawing on signaling theory and prior research on citizens' normative expectations of ideal public servants, this study employs a large language model to analyze 1825 job advertisements from health and transportation departments across seven U.S. states. Compared to the values citizens associate with ideal public servants in previous research, job advertisements predominantly emphasize values, such as expertise and dedication, while undersignaling relational values like serviceability, responsiveness, and honesty. Our findings suggest a misalignment between the values signaled in recruitment practices and those citizens associate with the ideal public servant. By adopting a citizen‐driven perspective, this study prompts scholars and public managers to question recruitment practices that may underemphasize values citizens prioritize in public servants, potentially limiting public administrations' ability to attract qualified candidates.

items.title: Cloud-deployable deep learning for smartphone-based body fluid cytology: a multi-architecture evaluation of YOLO and RT-DETR models
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate cytological evaluation of body fluid specimens is essential for diagnosing inflammatory and malignant conditions, yet manual interpretation remains labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. This study developed and deployed a smartphone-based deep learning framework for multi-class body fluid cell classification integrating object detection, ROI-based classification, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Three hundred Wright–Giemsa–stained cytospin slides, one per patient, were used to generate 7149 smartphone-acquired images, which were annotated and curated into seven predominant cell classes. To reduce data leakage, images were partitioned at the source-photograph (slide-field) level. Five detection architectures (YOLOv8n, YOLOv10n, YOLOv11n, YOLOv11n-seg, and RT-DETR) were trained and evaluated on a held-out test set. YOLOv11n-seg achieved the highest mAP@50 (0.840), mAP@50–95 (0.757), and precision (0.772), while YOLOv11n achieved the highest recall (0.823). For YOLOv11n-seg, confusion-matrix macro-F1 and weighted-F1 were 0.720 and 0.730, respectively. Eosinophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophils were among the better-recognized classes, whereas errors were more frequent among monocytes, macrophages, and mesothelial cells. Grad-CAM++ analysis showed that model activation was predominantly centered within cell regions but was interpreted only as supportive model-inspection evidence. A Streamlit web application demonstrated browser-based inference with detection overlays, cell counts, differential composition, and data export. The system should currently be regarded as research, educational, and decision-support prototype rather than a standalone diagnostic device. External validation with patient-level separation, multiple imaging configurations, and broader cell populations is required before clinical application can be considered.

items.title: Code-MUE: Measuring Code LLMs’ Uncertainty through Execution-Based Semantic Interaction Graphs
items.abstract: As Code Large Language Models (LLMs) become central to modern software engineering, their inherent stochasticity poses significant real-world risks, where even minor errors can lead to severe functional, security, or safety consequences. Reliable automation, therefore, demands the ability to distinguish between confident, well-supported predictions and stochastic guessing. However, existing uncertainty estimation methods face a critical gap: white-box and grey-box techniques are often inapplicable to closed-source models, while standard black-box text metrics fail to capture the unique fragility of code, where syntactic variation does not necessarily imply semantic divergence. To bridge this syntax-semantics gap, we introduce Code-MUE, a purely black-box framework that measures uncertainty through execution-based Semantic Interaction Graphs. Unlike prior approaches that rely on superficial textual similarity, Code-MUE grounds uncertainty in observable runtime behavior and calculates the von Neumann entropy of the solution space to quantify global semantic diversity. A large-scale empirical study across eight state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrates that Code-MUE achieves a strong negative correlation with functional correctness, with Spearman’s correlation reaching up to −0.98. It significantly outperforms lexical and embedding-based baselines while enabling robust risk detection and selective prediction in practical workflows.

items.title: Color discrimination in action: High-throughput measurement in immersive VR
items.abstract: Precise measurement of color discrimination across color space is limited by the time and effort required to collect large psychophysical datasets. We investigated whether immersive virtual reality (VR) can support high-throughput measurement of color discrimination without compromising data quality. A standard four-alternative forced-choice odd-one-out task was embedded in an interactive VR environment inspired by the rhythm game Beat Saber, in which participants indicated the location of a chromatic target by slicing approaching cubes. Stimuli were presented on a color-calibrated VR headset, and chromaticities were specified in DKL space. Discrimination thresholds were measured for hue and chroma shifts around two reference colors. Participants sustained response rates of approximately one trial per second while maintaining stable performance. Thresholds replicated established asymmetries in color discrimination: hue thresholds were lower than chroma thresholds, and the hue-chroma ratio differed between color quadrants. A control experiment comparing VR-based slicing responses with matched keyboard responses revealed comparable psychometric fits and threshold estimates, indicating that motor engagement did not degrade measurement precision. Questionnaire measures further showed significantly higher intrinsic motivation, enjoyment, and stimulation in the immersive condition relative to a classic static psychophysical task, without increases in reported pressure or discomfort. These results demonstrate that calibrated immersive VR can yield reliable color discrimination measurements at substantially increased throughput, providing a scalable approach for mapping the metric structure of color space.

items.title: Comments: New Horizons, New Challenges: ATCE 2026 Returns to Houston
items.abstract: It’s that time of year again in Houston. From 21 to 23 October, SPE will host thousands of oil and gas industry professionals at its 102nd Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) at the George R. Brown Convention Center. The theme of this year’s gathering is Exploring New Horizons with Innovative Solutions, which also serves as a call to action. Over the past decade, the industry has undergone tremendous change, and technology has often been central to how it has adapted. Over that span, we experienced the 2014 to 2016 oil price crash, which upended countless companies and led to massive layoffs across the industry. In January 2014, Brent crude traded above $107/bbl. A year later, it had fallen to little more than $50/bbl. The slide continued, and by January 2016 prices had dropped to roughly $32.50/bbl. The 2-year downturn that ushered in the era of “lower for longer” was driven in large part by the technological advances that enabled the rise of the North American shale revolution. Markets ultimately recognized that tight oil had materially altered the global supply picture. Just as the industry regained its footing, prices swung sharply again in 2018. Brent climbed to a 4-year high of about $86/bbl in October before falling to $50/bbl by December. During this downturn, particularly among US tight-oil and -gas producers, capital discipline became the defining business strategy as companies faced renewed pressure to improve returns while controlling spending. The pain was real. US oil and gas companies with significant shale exposure collectively lost nearly 30% of their value, while oilfield service providers saw approximately 40% erased from their market capitalization during the downturn. Few in the industry need to be reminded of the disruption that accompanied the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic that swept the industry off its feet just 1 year later. Economies around the world slowed dramatically. Highways emptied, airports went silent, and supply chains were broken. For those of us in the upstream sector, the market shock produced another seemingly unimaginable event. As Brent crude fell to about $14/bbl in April 2020, the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) briefly traded at negative prices, reaching –$37.63/bbl as storage constraints and market dislocation forced overextended traders to offload positions at almost any cost. But 2 years later, economies reopened and the pandemic receded. Negative oil prices became something of a historical anomaly. Then Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 sent energy markets into another period of turmoil, driving Brent crude above $125/bbl. That was 4 years ago. And prices retreated again as the world speculated that we were facing yet another oil glut. At the start of this year, many expected oil prices to settle into a range near $60/bbl. Instead, ongoing geopolitical tensions have once again defied market expectations. With the conflict between the US and Iran stretching out for more than 6 months, both Brent and WTI climbed above $100/bbl in September amid supply disruptions and growing concerns over global inventories. This brief walk down memory lane brings us back to ATCE’s theme this year of new horizons and innovative solutions. Over the past decade, the industry has repeatedly been forced to do more with less. The upside of these painful episodes is that producers today are more efficient than ever before and are generating record levels of production with fewer resources than many would have considered possible only a decade ago. But even as we look at $100/bbl oil prices today, few are cheering for them to go higher. The industry understands there is a breaking point for consumers and that demand destruction tends to have significant and lasting consequences. At ATCE, attendees will hear how some of the world’s leading energy producers are dealing with all this uncertainty, which many consider to be a hallmark of our new normal. Discussions will also address the industry’s effort to decarbonize while still helping billions of people get to work, keep their lights on, and heat their homes. Attendees will also learn more about the industry’s digital transformation, which has now been supercharged by the advent of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) programs, often referred to as frontier models. The rise of AI has been anticipated for years, but the widespread excitement, controversy, and debate surrounding its capabilities suggest that we are truly entering a new era of computing and software. Where AI ultimately leads us all remains difficult to predict. What is clear is that the industry’s mission remains unchanged. The business must continue to operate safely, remain resilient in the face of market uncertainty, and responsibly deliver the energy needed to fuel economic progress. New technologies, particularly AI, will play a major role in this effort if they are able to enhance human expertise and help organizations make better decisions. Several industry leaders will share their perspectives on these topics during ATCE’s Opening General Session. Moderated by 2026 SPE President Jennifer Miskimins, the panel will feature Ahmed Alebri, CEO of ADNOC Onshore; Peter Larden, senior vice president of upstream, conventional, and heavy oil for ExxonMobil; Lorenzo Simonelli, chairman and CEO of Baker Hughes; and Ezra Yacob, chairman and CEO of EOG Resources. Additional panels and technical sessions will explore topics including agentic AI, growing energy demand from data centers, and the challenge of improving recovery from unconventional reservoirs as many of the most productive US shale plays continue to mature. One more thing that attendees can expect to find in the SPE Pavilion this year is a special print edition of JPT, produced in partnership with the not-for-profit organization Project InnerSpace. The special issue features original JPT articles and technical paper synopses focused on next-generation geothermal systems. Our goal is to help oil and gas professionals better understand how the industry’s expertise, technologies, and decades of subsurface experience can contribute to the progress being made in this growing field of subsurface engineering. It is an exciting time for the oil and gas industry, but it is not free of major challenges. At ATCE, many of those challenges will be discussed and debated by the engineers, scientists, executives, and technical professionals working to identify practical solutions. I hope many of you will be part of those conversations and help shape the future of our industry when you return to your organizations. As I often do, I would also like to thank the many SPE members and volunteers who have devoted countless hours to organizing ATCE and the SPE’s other events throughout the year. Their efforts help make SPE the industry’s unrivaled forum for advancing petroleum engineering knowledge and sharing technical expertise. Much of that work takes place behind the scenes, but it is deeply appreciated by all of us at JPT. For more information about ATCE 2026 and to register, please visit the conference website.

items.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Occupational Health Control Strategies in Mitigating Chronic Disease Among Oil Drilling Workers
items.abstract: The hierarchy of controls framework prioritizes engineering solutions over administrative measures and personal protective equipment, yet oil drilling operations typically invert this approach. This mixed-methods comparative effectiveness study evaluated 400 workers across 15 drilling sites implementing different control strategies over 18 months. Engineering-dominant sites demonstrated 61% lower chronic respiratory disease incidence (HR=0.39, 95% CI: 0.23- 0.66) and 56% lower musculoskeletal disorders (HR=0.44, 95% CI: 0.28-0.69) compared to PPEreliant sites. Cost-effectiveness analysis revealed engineering controls achieved ₦19,840,000 ($12,400) per Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) gained versus ₦82,880,000 ($51,800) for administrative controls and ₦109,120,000 ($68,200) for PPE programmes. However, engineering control effectiveness degraded 47% over 18 months without adequate maintenance, while administrative compliance declined from 78% to 34%. Qualitative analysis identified six implementation barriers: capital investment resistance (87% of sites), production-safety conflicts (73%), maintenance system inadequacy (93%), management turnover disrupting continuity (67%), worker skepticism from past failures (73%), and chronic disease invisibility preventing urgency (93%). Findings demonstrate engineering controls' superior effectiveness and cost-efficiency while revealing that implementation sustainability determines real-world impact. Meaningful chronic disease prevention requires regulatory mandates prioritizing engineering solutions, adequate maintenance systems, organizational accountability for health outcomes, and long-term monitoring capturing delayed disease manifestations

items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Explainable AI Techniques for Histopathology-Based Cancer Detection Using Deep Learning
items.abstract: The analysis of histopathological images is an important method of diagnosing cancer. Deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks and transformer-based models have demonstrated great potential in automated cancer detection. However, they are black-box and cannot be understood in a clinical context. In this paper, a comparative study is conducted to analyze the explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approaches for cancer detection based on histopathology images on a hybrid model based on deep learning networks: ResNet-18 and Vision Transformer (ViT). The hybrid model is trained on histopathology images and three explainability mechanisms are used, including Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, and Score-CAM to visualize regions of decisions made. The created heatmaps are evaluated according to the accuracy of localization, noise minimization, and interpretability. Experimental results indicate that Grad-CAM++ provides better localization and Score-CAM generates more smooth and noisy explanations. This comparative analysis enhances transparency of models and helps to make more credible medical decisions.

items.title: Compiling Large Multi-modal Requirement Documents into Runnable Software Systems: From an Agentic Test-Driven Perspective
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved programming efficiency by parsing natural language into code snippets. However, their performance degrades significantly as requirements scale; when faced with multi-modal documents containing hundreds of scenarios, LLMs often produce incorrect implementations or omit crucial constraints. Observing LLMs' ever-evolving capability and their persistent stochastic hallucination, we raise a question: whether it is possible to make LLM-based agentic programming go beyond "code generation" to "requirement compilation", i.e., whether programmers can produce a runnable system by only accomplishing (non-trivial) requirement documents? In this work, we take a first step by proposing the ARC (Agentic Requirement Compilation) technique to parse a multi-modal requirement document, describing hundreds of scenarios in a DSL format, into a runnable software system. In addition to the source code, ARC also generates software engineering artifacts including (1) a modular design that spans the user interface, API interface, and database, (2) enriched test cases for each interface (including unit tests, modular tests, and integration tests), and (3) detailed traceability across all artifacts for software maintenance. Our approach employs a bidirectional test-driven agentic loop: (1) a top-down architecture phase that decomposes requirements into UI, API, and database interfaces, each of which is equipped with verifiable test suites, and (2) a bottom-up implementation phase where agents generate code that must satisfy the generated tests. Throughout this process, ARC maintains strict traceability across requirements, design, and code to facilitate intelligent asset reuse and follow-up maintenance. We evaluate ARC on two complementary benchmarks, i.e., a depth-oriented benchmark of 6 runnable web systems spanning 50-200 requirement scenarios, and the breadth-oriented AppForge benchmark comprising 101 Android app generation tasks. Across 3 independent trials, ARC outperforms all state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines, with the generated web systems passing on average 50.6% more GUI tests, and achieving 100% compile success and 68.3% test case pass rate on AppForge. In addition, a user study with 21 participants shows that participants with limited programming experience successfully write DSL-based documents consisting of 50 to 174 scenarios, within 5.6 hours on average, to generate a runnable system such as a real-world ticket-booking system of around 10K lines of code with maintainable architecture.

items.title: Confident but absent: AI use, self-efficacy for independent learning, and student absenteeism in higher education
items.abstract: Rising student absenteeism remains a persistent challenge in higher education, potentially exacerbated by the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Drawing on digital displacement theory, this study examines whether general AI use is associated with students’ self-efficacy for independent learning and absenteeism. Survey data from 291 Portuguese university students were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, explaining 38.7% of the variance in absenteeism and 34.4% in self-efficacy. Internal locus of control, peer influence, time management, and AI use emerged as significant predictors. General AI use was positively associated with both self-efficacy and absenteeism, suggesting that AI may strengthen independent learning confidence while coinciding with reduced face-to-face engagement. Multigroup analysis provided exploratory evidence of gender differences, with the AI use–self-efficacy relationship stronger among males at the 5% level, while other gender differences appeared only at a more lenient 10% threshold.

items.title: Contesting land-based greenhouse gas removal futures: Emerging sociotechnical visions of biochar in UK agriculture
items.abstract: Abstract This paper critically examines the emerging sociotechnical visions of biochar within UK agriculture, focusing on its potential role in greenhouse gas removal (GGR) and the broader net zero agenda. Agriculture is framed as both a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions and a unique sector capable of acting as a carbon sink, positioning it at the heart of debates about climate change mitigation. The paper adopts a sociotechnical visions framework to illuminate how stakeholders align with, contest, and propose alternatives to the dominant net zero sociotechnical imaginary. We identify two overarching sociotechnical visions of biochar in UK agriculture. The first is a sociotechnical vision of greenhouse gas removal through biochar produced at scale and applied to agricultural land, detailing both farmer alignment with and contestation of this approach. The second is a sociotechnical vision of biochar for multiple on-farm benefits, including farm business benefits, enhanced agricultural production and improved on-farm biodiversity. The analysis shows that the future of biochar in UK agriculture is characterised by diversity and contestation, requiring governance frameworks that accommodate multiple, sometimes competing, sociotechnical visions. This pluralism offers opportunities for more just, inclusive, achievable, and transformative pathways for biochar in UK agriculture. Additionally, the paper contributes to the literature on sociotechnical imaginaries and sociotechnical visions by foregrounding the dynamic interplay and negotiation between top-down institutional imaginaries—such as net zero—and emergent, grassroots visions developed by farmers and other agricultural stakeholders.

items.title: CT-Referenced Diagnostic Performance and Complementary Error Patterns of Artificial Intelligence Versus a Single Emergency Physician in Chest Radiograph Interpretation: A Retrospective Paired Diagnostic Accuracy Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support chest radiograph interpretation, but its clinical value depends not only on stand-alone accuracy but also on whether its errors differ from those of clinicians. We evaluated CT-referenced, target-specific diagnostic performance and complementary error patterns of a commercial chest radiograph AI system and a single emergency physician. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center, paired diagnostic accuracy study, 920 consecutive adults who underwent posteroanterior chest radiography and thoracic computed tomography (CT) within 4 h during the same emergency department encounter were included. A commercial AI system (hChestXR version 1) and a single blinded emergency physician independently assessed eight prespecified thoracic findings using CT as the reference standard. Paired differences were estimated with 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples and tested with exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Exact-target complementarity and simulated same-target OR/AND rules were secondary exploratory analyses. Results: Across 7360 patient–target assessments, including 1232 CT-positive findings, AI had significantly greater Holm-adjusted sensitivity for pneumothorax (90.8% vs. 50.8%), nodule/mass (63.3% vs. 32.7%), and rib fracture (77.2% vs. 46.5%). AI-only detections were most frequent for pneumothorax (47.7%), nodule/mass (44.9%), and rib fracture (43.6%), whereas physician-only detections were most frequent for atelectasis (24.8%), pulmonary edema (21.0%), and lung opacity (19.7%). In exploratory pooled analyses, sensitivity was 73.0% for AI and 62.0% for the physician. Exploratory simulated same-target OR/AND analyses demonstrated a sensitivity–specificity trade-off across pooled patient–target assessments but did not represent observed AI-assisted clinical performance. Conclusions: The AI system and the single emergency-physician reader in the study showed target-dependent, partly non-overlapping error patterns in this CT-selected emergency cohort. The findings support prospective multireader evaluation of AI as a second-reader tool but do not establish benefit from real-time AI-assisted interpretation.

items.title: Current State of AI in Surgery and Anesthesiology Selected Applications, Limits, and a Responsible Agenda for Latin America
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in surgery and anesthesiology encompasses different tasks: risk prediction, hypotension alerts, video analysis, technical-skill assessment, surgical-duration estimation, and postoperative support. Treating them as one promise of “AI surgery” obscures essential distinctions among retrospective performance, external validation, prospective clinical utility, impact on processes or outcomes, and routine implementation. This whitepaper synthesizes selected applications rather than exhaustively cataloguing all subspecialties, robotic platforms, or simulation techniques. The evidence closest to clinical evaluation in anesthesiology is concentrated in intraoperative hypotension prediction. A systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized-trial reports; its published total of 568 participants includes overlap between a study and its substudy and does not represent unique individuals. Seven reports evaluated the Hypotension Prediction Index and one evaluated fuzzy-logic control. The hypotension meta-analysis including the largest trial did not find a statistically significant difference and showed high heterogeneity. Favorable results from small trials do not establish universal benefit: this is a narrow family of systems, populations, and protocols. In surgery, phase recognition and technical-skill assessment have systematic reviews, whereas models for complications, delirium, length of stay, and surgical duration remain dominated by retrospective development or limited validation. Latin America has direct evidence that should not be replaced by silent extrapolation. A Bogotá study evaluated models for surgical-duration estimation; Brazilian studies developed models for postoperative delirium and length of stay after coronary artery bypass grafting; and LASOS described perioperative outcomes across 17 countries. These sources demonstrate regional research and data capacity and a measurable perioperative burden; they do not demonstrate general clinical effectiveness of AI, routine implementation, or transportability across countries. The directed search identified few regional AI records compared with the international literature; statements about infrastructure, interoperability, and governance therefore also rely on regional sources and are labelled as implementation context or inference, not model performance. Central finding: AI can currently support bounded perioperative surveillance, prediction, analysis, training, and operational tasks. It cannot yet responsibly promise independent intraoperative decisions, replacement of surgical or anesthetic

These designs were presented to the stakeholders during the co-creation workshops to enable them identify functionalities that were missing or those that were not important for them in discharging their mandates.
